name: I BEAN OF GREENIE BURGER (comes with black bean parsley puree)

recipe.history:
The black bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) is a variety of the common bean that has been cultivated in Mesoamerica for over seven thousand years, with archaeological evidence of its cultivation in Peru and Mexico predating written history by millennia. The bean was a cornerstone of the pre-Columbian agricultural tradition throughout Central and South America, where it formed the protein-rich foundation of diets alongside corn and squash in the classic Mesoamerican intercropping system known as the Three Sisters — a system in which each plant supports the others ecologically, the beans fixing atmospheric nitrogen that feeds the corn and squash while the corn stalk provides a trellis for the climbing bean. Spanish colonizers brought black beans back to Europe in the sixteenth century, and from there they spread to West Africa and Asia, but the bean never lost its deepest cultural roots: in Mexico, Cuba, Brazil, Venezuela, and throughout Central America, black beans remain a daily staple — frijoles negros, black bean soup, moros y cristianos — cooked in innumerable ways that reflect regional identity and family memory. Fresh flat-leaf parsley (Petroselinum crispum var. neapolitanum), while a Mediterranean herb of ancient Greek and Roman origin, has found its way into Latin American cooking as a brightening counterpoint to the earthiness of legumes, and the combination of black bean and parsley in a puréed sauce form represents a kind of culinary dialogue between the Americas and Europe.

Black beans came to American mainstream cuisine through multiple channels: the Cuban-American communities of Miami, the Mexican-American food culture of the Southwest, and the broader movement toward plant-based protein sources that accelerated in the late twentieth century. The black bean burger — a patty made entirely from seasoned beans — became a fixture on American restaurant menus by the 1990s, but this burger takes a different approach: the black bean parsley purée is a condiment, a sauce, a flavor layer applied to a beef burger rather than a replacement for the beef itself. This is not a compromise or a concession to any dietary philosophy; it is an acknowledgment that the earthy, almost chocolatey depth of a well-seasoned black bean purée is a magnificent partner for beef, providing a bass note that ketchup and mustard cannot approach. The parsley — blanched briefly to set its green color and blended into the purée — adds a sharp, clean, chlorophyll-forward brightness that keeps the sauce from becoming heavy or muddy.

I came to this preparation not through any grand concept but through an evening of ingredient improvisation that began with half a can of black beans and a large bunch of parsley I had bought intending to use for something else. I cooked the beans in olive oil with garlic, cumin, and smoked paprika until they were fragrant and slightly broken down at the edges, added the blanched parsley, a squeeze of lime, and blended the whole thing into a thick, intensely green-flecked purée. I tasted it and immediately thought: this needs beef. Not a salad, not a grain bowl — beef, specifically a medium-rare patty on a good bun. The combination confirmed itself with the first bite: the purée's earthy, slightly smoky depth amplified the savoriness of the beef in a way that was simultaneously subtle and unmistakable. I have made it dozens of times since, adjusting the ratio of bean to parsley to dial in the green-versus-earth balance, and the version I make today is quite dark green in color and very bright in flavor — unapologetically bold.

The black bean parsley purée is a sauce that reveals its best qualities when applied to a medium-rare patty. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit the patty's surface is hot enough to warm the purée on contact, releasing the volatile compounds in the parsley and the aromatic oils in the cumin and smoked paprika without cooking them away entirely. The fat rendered in the medium-rare beef absorbs and carries these compounds into every bite, creating an integrated flavor experience rather than a layered one. On an overcooked, dry patty the purée sits on the surface like paint, unable to penetrate the dry meat or interact with the minimal fat remaining. The medium-rare temperature is not a preference in this recipe — it is the physical condition under which the sauce and the beef can actually become one thing instead of two things sitting next to each other. Cook to 130 to 135. Rest. Spread the purée warm. Eat immediately.
ingredients: For the toasted sesame brioche buns (makes 4):
1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp milk (egg wash)
3 tbsp black sesame seeds for topping
For the black bean parsley purée:
2 cans (400g each) black beans, drained and rinsed (or 500g home-cooked black beans)
60g fresh flat-leaf parsley leaves (no thick stems), about 2 large handfuls
60 to 120ml vegetable broth or water, as needed
Freshly ground black pepper to taste
4 slices Pepper Jack or Monterey Jack cheese
1 avocado, mashed with lime juice, salt, and a pinch of cumin
1 cup fresh corn kernels (or defrosted frozen corn), charred in a dry pan
1 jalapeño, seeded and very finely diced
1 chipotle chile in adobo, minced, plus 1 tsp adobo sauce
instructions: 1. Make the black sesame brioche buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer with the dough hook. Add eggs and warm milk. Mix on low until combined, then increase speed and add softened butter gradually over 8 minutes. Knead until smooth and glossy.

2. Cover and refrigerate overnight. Next day, divide into 4 portions, shape into rounds, and proof on a parchment-lined baking sheet covered for 2 to 3 hours. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash, top generously with black sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.
3. Make the black bean parsley purée: Blanch parsley leaves in boiling salted water for 30 seconds. Transfer immediately to an ice bath. Drain and squeeze dry. This step sets the bright green color.
4. Heat olive oil in a saucepan over medium heat. Add garlic and shallot, cook 3 minutes until softened and fragrant but not browned.
5. Add black beans, cumin, smoked paprika, and cayenne. Stir and cook for 5 minutes until the beans are heated through and some have begun to soften at the edges.

6. Transfer bean mixture and blanched parsley to a blender. Add lime juice, salt, black pepper, and apple cider vinegar. Blend, adding broth or water as needed to achieve a thick, spreadable consistency similar to hummus — it should mound on a spoon but spread easily. Taste and adjust seasoning. The purée should be bold: earthy, smoky, bright green, and pleasantly sharp. Keep warm.
7. Make the chipotle crema: Stir together sour cream, minced chipotle, adobo sauce, lime juice, and grated garlic. Season with salt. Refrigerate until needed.

8. Char the corn: In a dry cast-iron or heavy skillet over very high heat, toss corn kernels for 2 to 3 minutes until they develop charred spots and a toasty aroma. Remove from heat. Combine charred corn with diced red onion, jalapeño, and cilantro. Season with salt and a squeeze of lime. Set aside.
9. Make the smashed avocado: Mash avocado with lime juice, a pinch of salt, and a pinch of cumin until slightly chunky. Keep covered with plastic pressed directly on the surface to prevent browning.

10. Prepare patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 170g). Shape into 3/4-inch-thick patties with a thumb dimple. Season both sides with kosher salt, black pepper, smoked paprika, and cumin just before cooking.
11. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side undisturbed.
12. Flip, immediately lay a slice of Pepper Jack on each patty. Tent with a dome. Cook 90 seconds to 2 minutes more.
13. Check internal temperature — pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a rack for 3 minutes.
14. While patties rest, split buns and toast cut-side down in the pan over medium heat for 60 to 90 seconds.
15. Assemble: Spread a generous 2 tablespoons of warm black bean parsley purée on the bottom bun.
16. Spoon smashed avocado on top of the purée. Place the rested, cheese-topped patty on top.
17. Spoon the charred corn salsa over the patty. Drizzle chipotle crema over the top.
18. Close with the top bun and serve immediately with lime wedges on the side.
